newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Winner of Irish poll to inherit booming economy.
newsitem.headline: Winner of Irish poll to inherit booming economy.

text.p: Whoever wins Ireland's June 6 election will inherit an economy which is surging ahead towards european Economic and Monetary Union at rates which are the envy of other EU states.

Spared the recession which chilled other European economies in recent years, all signs are that Ireland's is set to grow at exceptional rates into the next decade and slash unemployment from 11 to seven per cent by 2005.

Ireland's Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI) said last month that it expects GNP growth to average 5.5 percent a year in the second half of the 1990s, falling to five percent a year in the period 2000-2005.
Such growth would lift Ireland's economic performance into the first division of EU states after years of being seen as an underdeveloped backwater, the ESRI said.

"This implies that Ireland will approach the EU average standard of living around the middle of the next decade, probably exceeding that of the UK before 2005," the ESRI said in a medium-term review of the Irish economy.

The ruling "rainbow coalition" of Prime Minister John Bruton and the opposition led by Bertie Ahern's Fianna Fail are both committed to Ireland being a member of EMU from day one, despite the doubts of its biggest trading partner, Britain.

Such a move is seen as essential to help make Europe rather than London Ireland's centre of economic gravity and to continue to attract hi-tech foreign investment, which is lured by a 10 per cent corporation tax rate, they say.

Little separates the two blocs for the June 6 poll. The ruling coalition contains two left wing groups, the Labour party and the Democratic Left while Fianna Fail would be expected to form a government with the centre-right Progressive Democrats.
Both have expressed a determination to keep bringing down unemployment to the EU's lowest levels.
The ESRI says strong employment growth should lead to a substantial reduction in the jobless rate which the ESRI sees at around 8.6 percent by 2000 and at seven percent by 2005.
With prudent management of public finances, it should be possible to eliminate all new government borrowing in the next three years and even to run a small surplus by 2005, the ESRI says.
This would be sufficient to reduce Ireland's debt to GNP ratio to around 30 percent by the end of the next decade.

"The biggest danger domestically is that an excessive rise in expectations could feed into wage inflation or unsupportable demands on the exchequer. This would choke off the rapid growth at a premature stage," the review said.
But the institute said there could be an adverse impact on the Irish economy if European economic and monetary union (EMU) failed to go ahead.

"Given the economic and political capital invested in it at an EU level, there would probably be serious disruption of the EU economy, reflected in a substantial rise in interest rates in countries such as Ireland," the ESRI said.

Opposition and government are both concerned that if Britain stays out of EMU it will give sterling a competitive edge which will hurt Irish exporters but have said that the benefits of joining will in the long term outweigh such risks.
